question: Why do large vision transformers produce high-norm artifact tokens in their feature and attention maps, and can extra input tokens remove them?
hypothesis: Large, sufficiently trained models learn to recognize redundant patch tokens and use them to store, process and retrieve global information; giving the model explicit extra register tokens should remove the artifacts without hurting quality.
contributions: Identify and characterise high-norm outlier tokens in DINOv2, DeiT-III and OpenCLIP
Propose appending learnable register tokens to the input sequence, discarded at the output
Show registers remove the artifacts, set a new self-supervised state of the art on dense prediction, and enable LOST object discovery with larger models

method.summary: Diagnose outlier tokens by output norm in DINOv2 ViT-g, probe their content with linear models, then add N learnable register tokens after the patch embedding (like [CLS], dropped at output) and retrain DeiT-III ViT-B, OpenCLIP ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 ViT-L/14 with and without registers.

limits: Authors could not fully determine which aspects of training cause artifacts: 'we have not been able to fully determine which aspects of the training led to the appearance of artifacts'
Analysis of mechanism concentrated on DINOv2; hand-picked norm cutoff 150 'can vary across models'
OpenCLIP LOST gets slightly worse with registers; explanation (outliers in null space of value projection) left to future work
Register regularisation and quantised register norms left for future work
No hyperparameters, seeds or compute reported; single runs; training data sizes not given
Absolute OpenCLIP performance is lower due to the licensed-data corpus
MAE shows no artifacts but is weak for frozen features (75% linear probe, ViT-L)
